\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficients of a pointwise product]
\lean{FABL.fourierCoeff_pointwise_mul}
\label{FABL.fourierCoeff_pointwise_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourier_expansion, FABL.monomial, FABL.monomial_mul_monomial}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f,g:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and let $S$ be a
subset of the coordinates. The Fourier coefficient of the pointwise product $fg$ at $S$
is $\sum_{T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\widehat f(T\triangle S)\widehat g(T)$, where
all coefficients are taken with respect to the uniform measure and the
coordinate-product characters.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cardinality Bound for Symmetric Difference]
\lean{FABL.card_add_card_add_card_symmDiff_le_two_mul_dimension}
\label{FABL.card_add_card_add_card_symmDiff_le_two_mul_dimension}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$ and all subsets $S,T$ of an $n$-element set,
$|S|+|T|+|S\mathbin{\triangle}T|\le 2n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Three sets cannot all be large under symmetric difference]
\lean{FABL.not_three_large_of_eq_symmDiff}
\label{FABL.not_three_large_of_eq_symmDiff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.card_add_card_add_card_symmDiff_le_two_mul_dimension}
\difficulty{2}
Let $S,T,U$ be subsets of an $n$-element set. If $S=T\mathbin{\triangle}U$ and each of
$S,T,U$ has cardinality strictly greater than $2n/3$, then these conditions are
impossible.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficient of the square]
\lean{FABL.fourierCoeff_sq_eq_two_mul_empty_mul_of_large_support}
\label{FABL.fourierCoeff_sq_eq_two_mul_empty_mul_of_large_support}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_pointwise_mul, FABL.not_three_large_of_eq_symmDiff}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$, and let $S$ be a
nonempty subset of the coordinates whose Fourier coefficient for $f$ is nonzero. Suppose
every nonempty subset $T$ with nonzero Fourier coefficient for $f$ satisfies $2n<3|T|$.
Then the Fourier coefficient at $S$ of the pointwise square $f^2$ equals twice the
product of the constant Fourier coefficient of $f$ and its Fourier coefficient at $S$.
\end{theorem}
